title: Cramming for Exams? Experts Share Better Ways to Learn
paragraphs: If you're preparing for an exam — or just studying to keep up in class — your study routine probably involves taking notes as you're reading, and then going back over them. Maybe you pull out a highlighter.
However, while these old-fashioned study habits might work if you're cramming for a test, they actually do little to help with long-term learning.

Social media is full of study hacks, from chewing gum and smelling essential oils to listening to music — but these don't really work either, according to cognitive psychologist Pooja K. Agarwal, who studies how people learn.
She says those things might improve your mood and keep you awake, but they don't improve learning.
A more efficient way to learn is "retrieval practice," which involves recalling information instead of rereading it.

Rather than taking notes while reading, Agarwal suggests reading a few pages, then stopping and writing down what you remember before continuing. She says research shows this is one of the most powerful learning methods.

Retrieval practice can also involve explaining the material to a study partner or going over it in your head, says Henry L. Roediger, a cognitive psychology professor at Washington University in St. Louis.
Agarwal also recommends pausing before another study session to recall what you learned. Just write down everything you remember in a "brain dump," then think about what was most difficult, she says.
Spacing study sessions out over time can also help.

For example, if you cram for three hours right before a Friday exam, you might pass, but quickly forget the material. If you instead study one hour each on Monday, Wednesday and Friday, you'll do well on the exam and remember it better later, Agarwal says.
And Roediger says one of the most important learning tools isn't a study technique at all — it's a good night's sleep, which helps consolidate memories created during the day.
